title: "Divergent Hamiltonian transitions"

A [**divergent transition**](https://mc-stan.org/docs/reference-manual/mcmc.html) occurs when numerical integration error exceeds Stan's threshold. It indicates that a trajectory may not have followed the target geometry reliably in one region. We demonstrate the warning with a deliberately coarse computation on the same passage-level Student-t model used throughout this sequence.

The target geometry comes from the log [posterior](posterior-distributions.qmd), whose data contribution is the [likelihood](maximum-likelihood.qmd#probability-and-likelihood). [Correlation](../random-variables-and-distributions/correlation.qmd) can orient a narrow region, while [effective sample size](effective-sample-size.qmd#from-autocorrelation-to-ess) assesses dependence among retained draws; neither diagnostic substitutes for checking divergences in parameter space.

To see what the warning means, we will connect it to Hamiltonian energy error and compare adapted chains with deliberately coarse, unadapted transitions. We can then work out what to inspect when a divergence appears, instead of treating a change to one tuning parameter as an automatic repair.

## Energy error and geometry

HMC approximately preserves

$$
H(q,\rho)
=
-\log\widetilde f(q\mid\mathbf y)
+\frac12\rho^\mathsf TM^{-1}\rho.
$$

If a leapfrog trajectory begins at $(q,\rho)$ and ends at $(q^*,\rho^*)$, define

$$
\Delta H=H(q^*,\rho^*)-H(q,\rho).
$$

The HMC correction accepts with probability $\min\{1,\exp(-\Delta H)\}$. Small numerical errors are corrected by this accept--reject step. A divergence flags an energy error large enough that the discrete trajectory may have failed to represent the local geometry reliably.

An **interior point** lies away from the boundary of the parameter space, so a
sufficiently small move is possible in every coordinate direction. A target is
locally **regular** when its log density is finite and smooth enough near that
point for local slopes and curvature to describe nearby change. The
[derivative page defines those slopes](../random-variables-and-distributions/expected-values.qmd#derivatives-as-local-rates-of-change),
and the [posterior-grid page defines curvature through the
Hessian](beyond-conjugacy.qmd#hessian-as-local-curvature). These conditions can
fail or become numerically strained near a boundary, a sharp corner, or a
region where curvature changes rapidly.

Rapidly changing curvature can make one step size inaccurate in a narrow region even if it works elsewhere. In a hierarchical model, for instance,

$$
u_j\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau^2)
$$

can produce a narrow region when $\tau$ is near zero and a wider region when $\tau$ is large. A noncentered representation writes

$$
z_j\sim\mathcal N(0,1),
\qquad
u_j=\tau z_j.
$$

The two forms imply the same conditional distribution for $u_j$ at fixed $\tau$, but expose different numerical coordinates.

## Adapted and deliberately coarse transitions

The four chains examined on the preceding pages use NUTS after warmup has
adapted the step size and mass matrix. For comparison, we also generate
transitions for the same passage set, likelihood, priors, and initial region
after disabling adaptation, using a unit metric, fixing the step size at
0.03, and capping tree depth at 7. These deliberately coarse transitions let
us see the warning under unfavorable numerical settings; we do not use them
for posterior summaries.

Each change has a specific consequence. Without warmup, the step size and
mass matrix cannot adapt. The unit metric ignores posterior scale and
correlation, the fixed step size may be too large for the target, and the
depth cap limits trajectory work. The statistical model stays fixed while
the numerical approximation changes.

```{r}
#| label: load-provo-divergences
library(ggplot2)
library(posterior)

provo <- read.csv("data/provo/passage-summaries.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
cache <- readRDS(
  "data/provo/provo-stan-draw-cache.rds"
)

adapted_diagnostics <- as.data.frame(
  as_draws_df(cache$production_diagnostics)
)
coarse_diagnostics <- as.data.frame(as_draws_df(cache$stress_diagnostics))
coarse_parameters <- as.data.frame(as_draws_df(subset_draws(
  cache$stress_draws, variable = c("mu", "sigma")
)))
coarse_transitions <- merge(
  coarse_parameters,
  coarse_diagnostics[, c(".chain", ".iteration", "divergent__")],
  by = c(".chain", ".iteration")
)

divergence_summary <- data.frame(
  transitions = c("adapted NUTS chains",
                  "deliberately coarse unadapted transitions"),
  draws = c(nrow(adapted_diagnostics), nrow(coarse_diagnostics)),
  divergences = c(sum(adapted_diagnostics$divergent__),
                  sum(coarse_diagnostics$divergent__))
)
divergence_summary$rate <- divergence_summary$divergences /
  divergence_summary$draws

stopifnot(nrow(provo) == 55L,
          divergence_summary$divergences[1] == 0L,
          divergence_summary$divergences[2] > 0L)
divergence_summary
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-stress-divergences
#| fig-cap: "Deliberately coarse, unadapted transitions for the passage-level model. Accent points mark divergences; these transitions are not used for posterior summaries."
background_opacity <- .35
divergent_opacity <- .75
ggplot(coarse_transitions, aes(mu, sigma)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey68", alpha = background_opacity, size = .75) +
  geom_point(data = subset(coarse_transitions, divergent__ == 1),
             color = "#8B1A1A", alpha = divergent_opacity, size = 1.1) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-.015, .035), ylim = c(.025, .070)) +
  labs(x = "Passage-level contrast (mu)",
       y = "Passage contrast scale (sigma)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The adapted chains have `r divergence_summary$divergences[1]` divergences. The
deliberately coarse calculation has `r divergence_summary$divergences[2]`
among `r divergence_summary$draws[2]` transitions. The comparison shows the
diagnostic that appears when integration is degraded while the data and
posterior remain fixed.

## Responding to a real divergence

First locate the marked draws in theoretically relevant parameter pairs. Then
inspect parameter identification, predictor scales, and parameterization.
Recall that [identification asks whether the observable distribution
distinguishes parameter values](../experimental-design/index.qmd#what-you-should-already-know);
weak identification can create a long or narrow posterior ridge. Increasing
`adapt_delta` usually reduces step size and may repair modest integration
error; reparameterization may be needed when curvature changes substantially.
Refit and recheck all diagnostics.

The response sequence is thus: (i) locate the divergences, (ii) inspect scaling, identification, and parameterization, (iii) rescale or reparameterize when warranted, (iv) refit, and (v) recheck divergences, $\widehat R$, ESS, tree depth, and predictive behavior. Raising `adapt_delta` is one possible intervention within that sequence, not a substitute for it.

Filtering divergent iterations is never a repair. And a run with no divergence removes only this warning: chains may still disagree, have low ESS, or target a model that predicts the linguistic data poorly.

## Recap and forward link

1. Divergences flag large numerical energy error in particular target regions.
2. The deliberately coarse transitions change the numerical approximation
   while holding the model and data fixed.
3. Localized warnings may bias summaries even when their overall percentage is small.
4. Repair requires diagnosis, refitting, and rechecking rather than filtering transitions.

The [pairs-plot page](parameter-pair-plots.qmd#locating-the-stress-warning)
shows where the coarse-transition divergences occur in joint parameter space.

## Check your understanding

1. Which numerical quantity fails to remain approximately stable during a divergence?
2. Why do the deliberately coarse transitions tell us about computation
   rather than about a defect in the passage-level Student-t model?
3. Why might localized divergences matter even when their percentage is small?
4. When might reparameterization be more useful than only increasing `adapt_delta`?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The Hamiltonian, or total energy $H(q,\rho)$, fails to remain approximately stable. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The calculation deliberately disables adaptation and uses a coarse unit
   metric while holding the data and posterior fixed; it demonstrates
   numerical failure under those settings rather than a defective model. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. A small rate can be concentrated in a narrow, scientifically important posterior region, biasing summaries that depend on that region. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Reparameterization is more useful when posterior curvature changes sharply, as in funnel-like geometry that no single smaller step size handles efficiently. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
